  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons.
Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ‘ideation radius’ and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics.
To bridge this gap, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents.
Building on its predecessor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The AI Scientist</span>,)</cite>, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing.
Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of headless coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification.
The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage.
This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool, or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation.
Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
We further apply <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system’s capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research, including: a hypernetwork-based inductive bias for rapid Transformer adaptation and a meta-trained evolution strategy that matches or exceeds CMA-ES on 5 of 7 unseen Brax control tasks.
Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.
We open-source <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> and its figure generation tool, <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>, to aid collective development of automated (co-)scientist systems:</p>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Model (LLM)-based tool-calling agents can now complete increasingly long coding tasks with minimal human intervention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwa et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Computational research, however, is arguably more than a single long coding task: a practical system supporting human scientists must generate hypotheses, execute controlled experiments, validate claims, iterate on ideas, and communicate the results.
Existing AI scientist systems demonstrate parts of this loop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidgall et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jansen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpathy, 2026</a>)</cite>, but myopic hill-climbing can make agents behave merely as flexible hyperparameter optimization engines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferreira et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Van Stein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we tackle the systems-level gap between an agent that writes code and a system that can conduct reliable research.
We introduce <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> (<a href="#S0.F1" title="In The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), a human-steerable, agentic scaffold for end-to-end computational research.
The workflow drafts a task specification from a text description, coordinates parallel sandboxed workers, accumulates retrospective evidence, and writes a manuscript grounded in the results.
During the investigation phase, parallel workers revise scientific hypotheses in response to implementation failures, measured outcomes, and shared performance notes.
The resulting artifacts seed subsequent experiments and remain available for retrospective analysis, ablation design, and manuscript writing.
Predecessors of our system (<a href="#S1.T1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) relied on initial implementation directions and loose assessment of the idea implementation. This could result in weak experiment validation and overfitting. <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>, on the other hand, uses self-drafted rubrics-based verification and CLI agents for broader code edits and information protocols.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S1.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of Sakana AI’s AI Scientist Frameworks.<span id="S1.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
<span id="S1.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> enhances previous versions with rubric-based verification and the option for co-scientist enhancement.</span></span></figcaption>
<div id="S1.T1.7" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:639.8pt;height:61.2pt;vertical-align:-28.1pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(0.0pt,0.0pt) scale(1,1) ;">
<p id="S1.T1.7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Feature</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Codebase</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Execution</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parallel</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rubric-based</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Human Evaluation</span></span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td"></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Drafting</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Workflow</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiments</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Self-Verification</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Result</span></span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v1</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">Topic-Specific</span>

<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v2</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">Domain-General</span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">Tree-Based (AIDE)</span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">✓</span>

<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Agentic Scientist</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Domain-General</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Beam Search (CLI Agents)</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">✓</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">✓</span></span>
<span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S1.T1.7.1.1.1.5.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">Co-Scientist Conference Acceptance</span></span></span>
</span></span></p>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A development version of our system was used to automate parts of the research process on Error Diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fujita, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaneko, 2000</a>)</cite>. Afterwards, we submitted a single paper which was accepted as an ALIFE 2026 talk <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
We further demonstrate our framework across three Machine Learning research directions: our system discovers composition and optimization biases for hypernetwork-based LLM adaptation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Charakorn et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> also extends research on neural network-parametrized meta-black-box optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, yielding an optimizer now integrated in <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">evosax</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange, 2023</a>)</cite>.
Finally, our system manages to iteratively improve an RL-based LLM fine-tuning program by combining recent algorithmic advances.
All of these demonstrate the broad application of the system to enhance scientific knowledge beyond mere hill-climbing applications.
Our main contributions are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>, a (co-)scientist orchestration scaffold for human-steerable ideation, parallel execution, shared memory, rubric-based verification, and paper manuscript writing.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Co-scientist paper conference acceptance.</span> A paper created with assistance by <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> on backpropagation-free error diffusion learning algorithms was accepted at ALIFE 2026 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2026</a>)</cite> after limited human edits and verification.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-domain &amp; harness validation</span> spanning long-context LLM adaptation, evolutionary optimization, RL fine-tuning, and 5 additional domains. Across various tasks, model harnesses, and base models, our system managed to generate high-quality grounded research manuscripts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>, an agentic pipeline for editable scientific figure generation that outperforms PaperBanana on PaperBananaBench  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2026a</a>, <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="37.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>37.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">37.5</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25.0</annotation></semantics></math> overall score,)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background &amp; Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">End-to-end automated scientific discovery.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Research on LLM-driven science increasingly targets complete workflows rather than isolated steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Si et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
The <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v1</span> introduced a closed loop for proposing hypotheses, running experiments, analyzing results, and drafting manuscripts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, while The <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v2</span> removed human-provided code templates and introduced progressive agentic tree search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Ultimately, these developments combined with base LLM capabilities have led to end-to-end autonomous systems capable of producing workshop-level research content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Intology AI, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">AutoScience AI, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Agent Laboratory and AI-Researcher similarly connect literature analysis, experimentation, and report writing, with different opportunities for human feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidgall et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
CodeScientist combines literature and code search with code review, replication, and external assessment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jansen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, while CycleResearcher inserts automated review into the loop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and the AI co-scientist emphasizes scientist-guided hypothesis development <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gottweis et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
These systems vary in autonomy, search, and validation; here our focus is the reusable plus scalable orchestration and evidence layer that supports heterogeneous coding agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hill-Climbing via Program Evolution.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A complementary line casts discovery as search over executable artifacts.
FunSearch showed that language-model-guided program search can yield mathematical discoveries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Romera-Paredes et al., 2024</a>)</cite>; AlphaEvolve broadened evolutionary code search to algorithms and computational infrastructure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Novikov et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and ShinkaEvolve targets open-ended, sample-efficient program evolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
At a lighter weight, <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">autoresearch</span> uses coding agents to repeatedly edit and evaluate a training program under a fixed budget <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpathy, 2026</a>)</cite>, motivating direct comparison with classical hyperparameter optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferreira et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. ALE-Agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Imajuku et al., 2025</a>)</cite> demonstrated that simple beam search at sufficient scale provides a competitive harness for program optimization.
Across these approaches, the search unit is a program under a pre-specified objective.
Our scaffold uses such executable search within a broader hypothesis-to-report process: it broadens the scope of application by automating task drafting, validation rubric generation, and supporting objective creation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarking Research Agent Capabilities.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Research-agent benchmarks separate several capabilities that a single final score can obscure.
SWE-agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> established that the agent–computer interface strongly affects real-world coding performance.
MLAgentBench evaluates iterative machine-learning experimentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, whereas MLE-Bench covers longer-horizon engineering workflows involving data preparation, debugging, training, and optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; subsequent work studies how search strategy affects exploration and generalization in this setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Toledo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
At the research level, PaperBench measures replication of published AI work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Starace et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MLR-Bench targets open-ended machine-learning research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and EXP-Bench isolates whether agents can conduct valid AI experiments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kon et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al. (2024b)</a></cite> introduced an LLM-driven pipeline for paper reviewing, which was later validated on research papers published after the training data cutoff date <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Here, we make use of such automated proxy AI reviews and additionally report external reviews of the co-produced ALIFE submission as complementary evidence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Verification and Grounding.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Verification and communication are becoming explicit parts of agent design.
Rubric rewards can train AI co-scientists and provide feedback in domains without verifiable objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goel et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gunjal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Here, rubrics do not train the coding-agent backbone; instead, they serve as runtime contracts that ground each hypothesis to implementation checks and empirical evidence. The <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> manuscript drafting runs additional checks for facts and figures outlined in the paper. We discuss further related work in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Additional Related Work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> is a versatile agentic orchestrator scaffold for end-to-end computational <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">research campaigns</span> (<a href="#S0.F1" title="In The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
A campaign begins with a task specification, which researchers can provide directly or generate from a research brief with a drafting agent.
Then, the campaign proceeds through three phases: parallel investigation, retrospective evidence generation, and grounded paper writing.
Each phase runs as a separate process and feeds the next: the selected program and experimental artifacts produced by the first phase determine which baselines, ablations, and post-hoc analyses to run; the resulting evidence then grounds the manuscript. Finally, we leverage the previously introduced AI reviewer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> to provide proxy evaluation scores for the manuscripts.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Research Task Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before idea execution, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> requires an executable task specification that defines the research goal and its evaluation. This can either be specified manually or drafted agentically:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatleft" style="width:39%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/method_task_drafting.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:181/296;" width="181" height="296"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Task drafting workflow.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task specification.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A task specification comprises an initial program, a search evaluation program, an optional final evaluation program, and a machine-readable contract:
the initial program provides a deterministic baseline, while the search evaluation program determines whether a candidate program is correct, returns the scalar score used to rank and select candidates during the investigation phase, and records metrics and artifacts for later analysis.
When provided, the final evaluation program runs the selected program after exploration and reports post-search evaluation metrics.
The contract defines the candidate interface and evaluation procedures.
Tasks may additionally stage papers or code as research context, as in our hypernetwork adaptation and error-diffusion studies (<a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Open-Ended Architecture Research with The Agentic Scientist: Discovering Query-Conditioned Composition for Hypernetwork-Based LLM Adaptation ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a> and <a href="#S4" title="4 AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task drafting.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Researchers may provide the task specification directly or use the task drafting pipeline to create it from a human-written research brief (<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3.1 Research Task Setup ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
The pipeline has two main stages: a design agent converts the research brief into an experimental design, and a drafting agent converts this design into the task specification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The experimental design defines the method, candidate interface, compute budget, and protocols for search and final evaluations.
Before drafting begins, an independent review agent assesses the design and repairs any issues.
The drafting agent then implements the initial program, the search and final evaluation programs, and the task contract, while pinning dependencies and staging the required data.
The harness checks the contract and runs smoke tests of the evaluation programs before the alignment judge assesses scientific fidelity and verifies that the search and final evaluators are independent and use disjoint data.
In containerized runs, the production check additionally requires the initial program to complete the full search workload to ensure operational feasibility.
Failed scaffolds are repaired, and only versions that pass all checks proceed to parallel investigation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Parallel Investigation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The idea investigation phase spends a fixed budget of containerized research cycles across parallel workers, each exploring different hypotheses in a separate workspace while sharing distilled knowledge (<a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3.3 Contracted Research Cycles ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Multiple agent-based workers explore ideas in parallel, each advancing an independent sequence of research cycles.
These workers lease cycles from a synchronized queue, maintain separate run directories and worker-local best search score programs, which resemble a per-worker beam search.
A cycle starts with the worker importing the shared memory and the other workers’ distilled conclusions, and ends with the worker publishing new memory entries and updated conclusions to all other workers.
Communication occurs at cycle boundaries, while logs and program artifacts remain in worker directories.
At regular intervals, optional context pruning archives the histories and memory before resetting them, so that accumulated context does not bias subsequent cycles; the best program is carried into the next round to preserve progress.
After parallel execution, the aggregator merges worker histories and selects the best correct program found across workers. This selected program becomes the input to the retrospective evidence-generation phase.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Contracted Research Cycles</h3>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:38%;"><img src="2610.18933v1/method_parallel_loop.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:172/271;" width="172" height="271" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Investigation workflow.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each worker advances a sequence of research cycles, and each cycle runs two agents in turn: an ideation agent and an execution agent.
The ideation agent turns one hypothesis into a typed contract, and the execution agent then tests that contract against the evaluator, so that intent and evidence remain separate(<a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3.3 Contracted Research Cycles ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ideation agent.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At the start of a cycle, the ideation agent receives the task, recent idea and attempt histories, the manifest for the worker’s best program, and distilled conclusions.
The protocol requires inspecting this context without experimenting or modifying candidates (‘read-only’).
The ideation agent must instead emit a structured idea bundle containing a title, a falsifiable hypothesis, an ordered implementation plan, and the target rubrics.
Those records are normalized, and any missing fields or mismatched rubric identifiers are rejected.
This boundary records the idea as a structured artifact, so the execution agent does not have to reconstruct its intent from conversational context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Execution agent.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The accepted contract, evaluator, task files, and the worker’s best program are staged into an experiment workspace.
The execution agent creates append-only candidate variants and follows an edit–evaluate–verify loop within a fixed evaluation budget, producing metrics, correctness checks, and rubric evidence.
Two distinct gates are then applied: an all-rubric-pass attempt marks the contract complete, whereas updating the worker’s best program requires a correct candidate with a strictly higher score; rubric completion and updates to the worker’s best program are therefore independent decisions.
All logged idea provenance and attempt outcomes are retained and later condensed to guide interpretation during paper writing.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Retrospective Evidence Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This phase studies the selected program from the investigation phase in depth: (1) it runs controlled baselines and ablations that isolate the idea effects, and (2) it derives post-hoc analyses that characterize the behavior of the method on the considered task.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Controlled baselines and ablations.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The selected program is first instrumented with additional metrics, such as extra scores and time series data, so that every generated baseline and ablation can be compared in detail on common ground.
Given the code diff between the selected and initial programs, an agent then proposes baselines and ablations with explicit hypotheses and implementation plans, where each ablation must isolate an innovation introduced by the selected program.
A separate agent filters these proposals for relevance, feasibility, and single-change scope.
Each validated plan receives an isolated workspace and follows an agent-guided edit–evaluate–verify loop that modifies the selected program to implement the intended change and score it against the evaluator, alongside the unchanged selected and initial programs.
The evaluator can be run for multiple seeds to make comparisons statistically meaningful, and their summaries and metrics are aggregated across seeds, ablations, and baselines by task.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Post-hoc analysis.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The post-hoc pipeline proposes, filters, executes, and aggregates diagnostics that characterize the behavior of the frozen selected program on the considered task.
Diagnostics may run new inference or analyze existing artifacts, such as checkpoints and logs.
Programmatic checks reject proposals that retrain or otherwise alter the selected program, or require unavailable artifacts.
When no usable checkpoint exists, an optional bootstrap stage enables checkpoint saving and reruns the evaluator once; all subsequent analyses keep the resulting version frozen.
The resulting post-hoc analyses, together with the baseline and ablation results, form the evidence that the paper writing phase turns into empirical claims.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Grounded Paper Writing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The paper writing phase converts the outputs of the preceding phases into a manuscript through an artifact-grounded workflow that reviews and audits claims made in the paper (<a href="#S3.F4" title="In 3.5 Grounded Paper Writing ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatleft" style="width:38%;"><img src="2610.18933v1/method_grounded_reporting.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:181/216;" width="181" height="216" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Evidence-to-paper pipeline.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evidence staging and planning.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We merge worker results into aggregate outputs and stage them in a dedicated workspace, with a memory summary and raw artifacts.
Quantitative claims resolve to those outputs and raw artifacts, while the memory summary only guides interpretation.
Before and after drafting, reference planning retrieves bibliography entries (<a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Bibliography Retrieval ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on The Agentic Scientist ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>). An optional stage fixes the central thesis, result emphasis, and figure plan.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Manuscript generation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The writer agent produces a compilable LaTeX manuscript together with a claim-to-source map and figure manifest, whose plots are derived from staged workspace results.
The strategy may also request <span id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>, our agentic figure generation pipeline (<a href="#S3.SS6" title="3.6 autoillustrate: Conceptual Diagram Generation ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.6</span></a>), to produce a conceptual overview diagram.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Validation and review.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At the end of our pipeline, a single repair loop alternates deterministic checks with agent judgment and feeds any failures back to the writer agent for revision.
The validation checks cover structural completeness, provenance and claim-to-source links, compilation, and venue and page budget constraints.
An independent audit agent runs every round on a read-only copy of the workspace and flags where the paper’s numbers, comparisons, or conclusions overclaim or contradict the canonical data and evidence trail.
An optional reviewer-style agent assesses framing, caveats, figures, and clarity, and may ask the writer agent to narrow or qualify claims.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span><span id="S3.SS6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>: Conceptual Diagram Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> is designed around two requirements: scientists should be able to modify conceptual figures, and they should represent the methodology faithfully.
To meet these requirements, the pipeline first produces an editable <span id="S3.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> diagram to ground the figure’s structure, which is later exported and augmented using a separate image generation model.
As illustrated in <a href="#S3.F5" title="In Composition, enhancement, and verification. ‣ 3.6 autoillustrate: Conceptual Diagram Generation ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the concept generator runs a six-phase pipeline that turns a method brief into a multi-panel figure whose layout source remains explicitly editable.
Unless stated otherwise, all papers generated by our system in this work have their main conceptual figure generated by <span id="S3.SS6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Editable panel generation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The pipeline begins with a planning agent that reads the staged source and instructions and describes the panels within one top-level configurable layout.
A styling agent then defines a shared color palette and typography specification to keep independently rendered panels consistent.
Rendering agents create the panels independently and in parallel as editable <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> diagrams.
Each agent relies on a template to define the panel topology and a Python generator script to compute coordinates and check bounding boxes for overlap.
Visuals that <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> cannot produce remain as placeholder boxes.
When possible, a generated <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">matplotlib</span> script fills these boxes; the enhancement stage handles any remaining placeholders.
A vision-model audit then evaluates each panel for rendering fidelity, factual accuracy, and sufficient detail.
When the inspection detects a defect, the pipeline edits the source, rebuilds the panel, and repeats the audit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Composition, enhancement, and verification.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After all panels pass, the pipeline composes them into a single editable <span id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> source and exports a raster version.
An image generation model restyles the raster export, after which a final verification step compares the enhanced candidate with the editable reference and repeats the checks defined during panel inspection.
Any discrepancy triggers another source-editing, export, enhancement, and verification pass.
After several repair passes, the pipeline returns the enhanced candidate with the strongest verification results.
If no candidate passes verification, the pipeline returns the raster export from the editable source.
Because the pipeline preserves this source throughout the process, scientists can revise the content or layout directly without regenerating the figure.
We provide additional details in <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E autoillustrate: Supplementary Material ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/figures/autoillustrate_pipeline.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/201;" width="471" height="201" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">autoillustrate<span id="S3.F5.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> pipeline<span id="S3.F5.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">, generated by <span id="S3.F5.10.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> itself. </span>(A)<span id="S3.F5.10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Six phases turn a document and an instruction into an editable <span id="S3.F5.10.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> figure: LLM sub-agents decide content, while deterministic Python owns geometry and the generative image model only restyles. </span>(B)<span id="S3.F5.10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> In Phase 2, panels are rendered from a combination of automatically-generated templates whose coordinates are determined by LLM-generated Python code. </span>(C)<span id="S3.F5.10.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> In Phases 5–6, the enhanced candidate with the best audit results is selected; if none is acceptable, the deterministic render is used as a fallback.</span></span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We validated a development version of our system within a co-scientist setting: <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> was used to automate parts of the research process targeting the extension of a backpropagation-free neural network training method.
After thorough human verification and manuscript edits, we submitted a single paper to ALIFE 2026, which was accepted after external peer review as a main conference talk.
We emphasize that this single submitted ALIFE paper was produced by human researchers using <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> as a tool, and not submitted as an unaltered system output. The human authors remain responsible for its methods, claims, authorship, and disclosure.
In this section, our focus is to describe the process by which experimental outputs became a submitted manuscript and were subsequently revised for the camera-ready version (<a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4 AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/figures/alife_camera_first8pages.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/300;" width="471" height="300" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Camera-ready ALIFE 2026 paper after the single submitted manuscript was accepted. The full manuscript and additional details can be found in <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Error Diffusion ALIFE Paper Details ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>A Human-Supervised Research Workflow</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The project began with a human-selected research direction: investigating how Error Diffusion (ED) could be extended beyond its earlier demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaneko, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fujita, 2026</a>)</cite>. ED leverages a three-factor learning rule (presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity, and a globally broadcast error signal) originally studied in a dual-stream setting with paired excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) neurons. We chose to illuminate this research direction together with <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> since it investigates the following question: how can classical biologically-inspired learning algorithms be revived with modern deep learning techniques?</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Human researchers specified the scientific objective and the constraints for a valid implementation.
Within that contract, <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> proposed candidates, implemented training procedures, ran experiments, inspected failures, and generated plots.
The human researchers selected benchmarks (see creation process overview in <a href="#S4.F7" title="In 4.1 A Human-Supervised Research Workflow ‣ 4 AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) and specified initial rubrics:
A numerically strong result was not treated as evidence of progress unless its implementation also satisfied the rubric constraints.
For example, one rubric prohibited hidden credit assignment through automatic differentiation or transposed forward weights. This required the positive and negative streams to remain distinct dual-stream, and specified the intended local information available to an update.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/human_intervention_flow.svg" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/106;" width="471" height="106"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S4.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Creation process of the ALIFE paper: human researchers defined the initial direction, baseline, and rubrics; supported the experiment domain transition; verified results, references, and claims before submission; and incorporated reviewer feedback into the camera-ready paper.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Summary of Discovery and Dynamics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> first extended ED from binary to multiclass classification: during the parallel investigation phase, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> developed <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">modulo error routing</em>, a structured mechanism for assigning multi-class output errors to hidden units.
This enabled multiclass learning while preserving the dual-stream, Dale-constrained architecture, in which weight signs remain fixed throughout training.
Subsequent experiments focused on robustifying learning dynamics: <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> identified layer-specific sigmoid widths, batch-centered error signals, and asymmetric E/I initialization as important stabilizers, raising accuracy to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="96.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>96.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> on MNIST <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun et al., 1998</a>)</cite> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="61.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>61.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">61.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> on CIFAR-10 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky et al., 2009</a>)</cite>.
Ablations further showed that the individual contributions were task-dependent: widened sigmoids were critical on MNIST, whereas batch-centering became substantially more important on CIFAR-10.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At this stage, human researchers transferred the best-performing ED implementation from the MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments to the RL setting, and prepared the Brax <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freeman et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and Craftax <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Matthews et al., 2024</a>)</cite> environments.
For RL experiments, an additional methodological constraint was added to the rubrics: the method was required to retain the PPO objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, while using the gradient of the PPO loss with respect to the logits as the output-level error signal for Error Diffusion.
Within this constraint, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> adapted the dual-stream ED mechanism to PPO and explored the resulting ED-PPO variants.
ED-PPO achieved performance comparable to standard baselines on several Brax tasks, although its performance was less consistent on Humanoid and Craftax (see figures in ALIFE paper manuscript; <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Error Diffusion ALIFE Paper ‣ Appendix C Highlighted Papers (Co-) Generated by The Agentic Scientist ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Post-hoc analyses linked these results to the dynamics of credit assignment: local update signals weakened substantially in earlier layers, while training shifted E/I ratios toward balance.
In summary, the results obtained demonstrate that ED generalizes beyond its original binary-classification setting. The mechanisms required for effective learning depend on task difficulty and domain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Human Result Verification &amp; Manuscript Edits</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before submission to ALIFE, researchers verified the generated research artifacts.
This included checking that the generated implementations matched the scientific hypotheses being tested, confirming that the reported tables and figures accurately reflected results produced by the corresponding code, and revising the manuscript where the generated text overstated or inaccurately characterized the evidence.
For example, human researchers added appropriate statistical analyses and, when the results showed comparable performance, revised claims such as “ED-PPO significantly exceeds BP-PPO” to “ED-PPO performs on par with BP-PPO”.
Additionally, all references in the BibTeX bibliography were manually verified to ensure that the cited works existed and supported the statements for which they were cited.
During this process, human researchers removed several citations that did not support the corresponding claims, and added important references omitted from the generated manuscript.
These included the reference to the original ED work, which is available only through an archived webpage.
The generated manuscript was treated as an intermediate research artifact, which was modified by human researchers, improving the writing of several sections (e.g., future work, etc.). We then submitted this single paper to the ALIFE 2026 conference.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Peer Review, Camera-Ready Paper Revisions</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This submission process illustrates the AI co-scientist approach enabled by our system: outputs were not just optimized code or isolated experimental reports, but a coherent working paper making a scientific claim, positioning it relative to prior work, and presenting evidence across multiple domains. We emphasize that only a single paper was submitted after our careful manual verification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The subsequent ALIFE peer review process provides external evidence for the quality of the co-created paper submission.
Overall, the paper was accepted as a talk, with individual recommendations of <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Strong ACCEPT</span>, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weak REJECT</span>, and <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weak ACCEPT</span>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Reviewer 1</span> framed the work as a relevant artificial-life contribution, as it evaluates the consequences of a biological assumption, Dale’s principle, and found the methods and results technically sound.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Reviewer 2</span> highlighted that the neuroscience connection of the work was interesting but questioned whether the paper would better fit a neural network venue. Additionally, they asked for clearer explanations of notation, matrix conventions, modulo indexing, and technical details. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Reviewer 3</span> was positive and requested more intuition about ED updates, non-negative activations, per-neuron error signals, baseline comparisons, ED-PPO architecture, and the meaning of gradient attenuation without backpropagation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We afterward used this feedback to enhance the camera-ready version of the manuscript: the post-acceptance changes are best characterized as targeted scientific clarifications rather than a change in the underlying study.
In particular, the camera-ready version tightens several claims about prior ED results, adds Dale-compliant reinforcement-learning results, corrects the Error Diffusion citation context, clarifies that Direct Feedback Alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nøkland, 2016</a>)</cite> routes errors through fixed random matrices, and cleans up the dual-stream architecture description and ED update equation.
It also replaces potentially misleading gradient language with “proxy” or “local surrogate” gradient terminology, refines the biological interpretation of E/I balance, repositions the discussion of Craftax and the dual-stream parameter overhead, and fixes typographic details such as quotation marks.
These edits make the paper more precise about biological plausibility and local learning while leaving the empirical evidence and overall narrative intact.
Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Human Result Verification &amp; Manuscript Edits ‣ 4 AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes human intervention throughout the manuscript-development process.
In summary, this study provides evidence of <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> being capable of supporting researchers to explore unorthodox AI topics across the entire research process.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Evaluating <span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> across five manually prepared research tasks that span optimization, representation learning, and predictive modelling. Each campaign starts from a task specification with different research objectives, starting points, and search iteration resources (see <a href="#S5.T3" title="In Task, harness, and model sweep. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for the task suite overview).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task, harness, and model sweep.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run the task sweep across four agent harnesses: Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and OpenCode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Earendil Works, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anomaly Innovations, 2026</a>)</cite>. Codex and Claude Code each use four assigned models, while Pi and OpenCode each use three, all at high reasoning effort (<a href="#A7.T10" title="In G.1 Aggregate Sweep ‣ Appendix G Task Properties and Hyperparameters ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>). Each run uses 20 idea investigation iterations and concludes with a written manuscript. Here, we focus on aggregated insights and provide more details on task-specific settings and discoveries can be found in <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Details on Aggregated Sweep Task Discoveries ‣ Appendix B The Agentic Scientist: Additional Results ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Paper-level evaluation protocol.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All generated research runs share the same scoring function within a task instance and can thereby be directly compared on their numerical optimization outcome. Additionally, we use the AI Reviewer’s <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> 1–10 <em id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Overall</em> score as a paper-level proxy metric:
For each generated manuscript, five separate calls to <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini-2025-04-16</span> review the extracted PDF text using NeurIPS-style guidelines and a fixed in-context example of a paper–review pair. A sixth call acts as an area chair to synthesize the reviews.
The original study in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al. (2026)</a></cite> validated the reviewer against acceptance decisions for ICLR submissions from OpenReview, including a post-training-data-cutoff 2025 cohort.
We note that the AI reviewer score solely serves as a proxy for reviewer-perceived paper quality, and not as ground-truth evidence of full scientific correctness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model capability, harness impact, and paper quality.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generally speaking, newer model releases tend to be associated with higher reviewer scores (<a href="#S5.F8" title="In Model capability, harness impact, and paper quality. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>a). When evaluating the models within their respective native coding harnesses, this observation appears to be more strongly pronounced for Claude- than GPT-based models.
Matched-model comparisons show minor performance differences across harness choice, while the underlying model matters more (<a href="#S5.F8" title="In Model capability, harness impact, and paper quality. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>b). No harness is uniformly best. OpenCode ranks lowest with GPT-5.6-Sol but highest with Opus 5 and DeepSeek-v4-Flash. The model developers’ own harnesses offer no consistent advantage: Codex ties Pi with GPT-5.6-Sol, and Claude Code falls between OpenCode and Pi with Opus 5.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/reviewer_score_vs_release_date.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153"></object>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Search progress and rubric dynamics.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The search traces show gains in best observed scores alongside fluctuating rubric pass rates. Final performance is positively associated with reviewer scores on four of the five tasks, most strongly for hyperparameter optimization, while learned optimization shows little association (<a href="#S5.F9" title="In Search progress and rubric dynamics. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).
Pooling all 70 campaigns after converting both final performance and reviewer scores to within-task percentile ranks gives a positive aggregated association (<math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.44</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.44</annotation></semantics></math>; <a href="#S5.F8" title="In Model capability, harness impact, and paper quality. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>c).
This observation is consistent with manuscript reviewer scores tracking measured numerical performance.</p>
