<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Additional Case Studies: Putting <span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> to work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> on three case studies: Language model adaptation (<a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Open-Ended Architecture Research with The Agentic Scientist: Discovering Query-Conditioned Composition for Hypernetwork-Based LLM Adaptation ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>) through hypernetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Charakorn et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, evolutionary optimization (<a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Open-Ended Algorithm Discovery with The Agentic Scientist: Meta-Evolving CMA-Anchored Learned Evolution Strategies ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>) through meta-learned neural network parametrizations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, and language model RL fine-tuning (<a href="#S6.SS3" title="6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.3</span></a>) on mathematical reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Open-Ended Architecture Research with <span id="S6.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>:  Discovering Query-Conditioned Composition for Hypernetwork-Based LLM Adaptation</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this experiment, we explore how <span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> can autonomously write an insightful scientific paper after successfully investigating a specific topic. As a case study, we choose the recently published hypernetwork-based LLM adaptation work from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Charakorn et al. (2026)</a></cite>, <em id="S6.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Doc-to-LoRA</em>. Unlike the other settings, <span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> is given the Doc-to-LoRA paper’s LaTeX source and its public code repository as the starting point.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/doc_to_lora_search_dynamics.png" id="S6.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/148;" width="476" height="148" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F10.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="S6.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(Left) Search trajectories for Doc-to-LoRA scientist runs given 40 idea iteration budget with Codex + GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude + Opus-5, and Pi + DeepSeek-V4-Pro on the multi-NIAH task. Both Codex and Claude runs improve steadily on the task. (Right) Exact-match accuracy is shown as a heatmap grouped by the number of test sample needles. Red crosses indicate invalid iterations.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Problem formulation.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Doc-to-LoRA introduces a hypernetwork that outputs low-rank adaptation (LoRA) matrices for a target LLM given a textual document. The generated LoRA serves as a weight-distilled knowledge bank and can be used to update the target LLM for document-based question answering without the need to place the documents in the LLM’s context window.
To handle documents beyond the context length of its encoder model, Doc-to-LoRA splits long documents into chunks and generates one LoRA independently for each chunk.
The standard approach concatenates the per-chunk low-rank factors into a higher-rank LoRA. However, naively combining multiple LoRAs can cause interference between several facts induced by different chunks.
Here, we focus on multi-needle-in-a-haystack (multi-NIAH) retrieval as a proxy task: each context contains one to four named facts, but the prompt asks for only one target needle’s four-digit number. To be successful at this task, a trained hypernetwork must avoid multi-LoRA interference via compositional LoRA designs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Needle-in-a-haystack task setup.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Any modification proposed by <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> is limited to architectural or training-related edits given a fixed encoder <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemma-2-2b-it</span> model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2024</a>)</cite>, fixed data generation, fixed evaluation scripts, and a 3-hour single-GPU training time budget.
The evaluation spans five context-length bins from short up to <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65{,}536" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>65,536</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65{,}536</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, with needles randomly placed at random positions. Given the resulting Doc-2-LoRA weights, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, the investigation target for <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> is the exact-match accuracy on the queried number:</p>
<table id="S6.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> search dynamics.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ran <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> for 40 idea-investigation steps with three model-harness combinations (<a href="#S6.F10" title="In 6.1 Open-Ended Architecture Research with The Agentic Scientist: Discovering Query-Conditioned Composition for Hypernetwork-Based LLM Adaptation ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).
The Claude and Codex variants both reach near-optimal scores, with Claude improving faster.
In contrast, Pi + DeepSeek-v4-Pro’s run shows fewer but larger jumps and plateaus below 50%.
In the Claude run, the generated report organizes the proposals by the mechanism each one tests: architecture redesign, auxiliary training objectives, LoRA merge weighting, and query-conditioned composition.
The key discoveries are as follows: redesigning the architecture or adding auxiliary objectives yields little gain, whereas query-conditioning the LoRA composition alone raises accuracy to <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Adding query-relevance filtering with delimiter-aligned chunk boundaries reaches <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S6.F11" title="In The Agentic Scientist search dynamics. ‣ 6.1 Open-Ended Architecture Research with The Agentic Scientist: Discovering Query-Conditioned Composition for Hypernetwork-Based LLM Adaptation ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>).
The generated paper therefore concludes that the bottleneck is not adapter-generation capacity or the training loss: multi-needle Doc-to-LoRA retrieval is a routing problem, in which the system must decide, based on the query, which chunk’s adapter to activate when merging multiple adapters.
The full paper written by <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> and its AI review are presented in <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Doc-to-LoRA Query-Conditioned Selection Paper &amp; AI Review ‣ Appendix C Highlighted Papers (Co-) Generated by The Agentic Scientist ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

(a) Hypernetwork’s head redesign, auxiliary objective, and unconditional merging stay at or below the <math id="S6.F11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="51.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>51.7</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">51.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> exact-match accuracy, while query-conditioned composition reaches <math id="S6.F11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.0</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>. (b) Starting from the query-blind (unconditional) merge, query-dependent merging provides a significant improvement; relevance-based text placement and delimiter-aligned chunking close the remaining gap.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Discovered Inductive Biases.</span> <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> demonstrates that naively composing every generated adapter makes the target LLM conflate multiple facts. The main failure mode is responding with a distractor number rather than the queried one. The successful idea is to make the adapter merging query-conditioned: <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> proposes an interaction score between the query and each chunk that selects the right adapter at composition time, without adding trainable parameters or changing the training objective.
<span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> then adds two smaller but complementary structural changes: relevance-based text processing and delimiter-aligned text chunking.
Relevance-based text processing removes the noise tokens around the token span most relevant to the query, so the adapter is generated from the queried fact, instead of the neighboring haystack.
Delimiter-aligned text chunking keeps each needle sentence intact before the query-conditioned address is computed.
We note that the <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> demonstrated that this inductive bias works well with the multi-needle-in-a haystack task. Future work should investigate the generalization of the discovered mechanisms beyond this synthetic long-context retrieval task.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Open-Ended Algorithm Discovery with <span id="S6.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>: 
<br class="ltx_break">Meta-Evolving CMA-Anchored Learned Evolution Strategies</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Black-box optimization (BBO) is an established target for automating algorithm discovery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite>: compact update rules determine sampling distributions, solution recombination, and covariance adaptation. But coordinating these mechanisms remains difficult <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shala et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
One line of prior work focused on learning attention-parametrized evolutionary algorithms (EA) through meta-BBO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Faldor et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
Here, we ask whether <span id="S6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> can improve the meta-optimizer program itself (i.e., perform ‘meta-meta-BBO’).</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task setup.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of this research campaign is to design a better procedure for obtaining a learned evolutionary algorithm.
Each program proposed by <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> is judged by how well its learned EA generalizes to unseen tasks. Evaluation proceeds in two steps: (1) the EA’s neural network parameters are meta-trained on a set of synthetic tasks, and (2) the resulting frozen parameters are evaluated on a separate held-out task.
For meta-training, we use CMA-ES <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001</a>)</cite>: at each generation, a random subset of BBOB  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hansen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> tasks is sampled, and the program runs optimization for a population of EA parameters. The best task-specific objective values reached by an EA instance are aggregated into a single meta-training score.
After meta-training completes, the final CMA-ES mean is frozen and evaluated on a validation task: the learned EA algorithm evolves a linear policy on a robotic control task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freeman et al., 2021</a>, Brax Ant-v1,)</cite>.
This evaluation tests the generalization capabilities to new tasks and optimization budgets (2,000 generations with a population size of 256). The agent-level search score is defined as:</p>
<table id="S6.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{score}=\left(\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{candidate}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{initial}}\right)/\left(\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{CMA\text{-}ES}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{initial}}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>score</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>AUC</mi><mi>candidate</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>AUC</mi><mi>initial</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>AUC</mi><mrow><mi>CMA</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ES</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>AUC</mi><mi>initial</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{score}=\left(\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{candidate}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{initial}}\right)/\left(\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{CMA\text{-}ES}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{initial}}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where AUC is the mean of the 2,000-point best-so-far return curve.
The synthetic tasks are exclusively used to train the weights of an <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> EA proposal, while the validation Ant evaluation measures task generalization and scores optimizer programs across agent iterations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/figures/metaevo_codex_vs_claude_30.png" id="S6.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:440/137;" width="440" height="137" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F12.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 12</span>: </span><span id="S6.F12.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Search trajectories for 30 idea iterations with GPT-5.6-Sol + Codex, Opus-5 + Claude, DeepSeek V4 Flash + Pi, and Kimi K3 + OpenCode.
Dots are individual Ant search-validation evaluations and step curves are the cumulative best.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> search dynamics.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All four considered <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> configurations obtain a normalized search score above one, indicating that each achieves a higher AUC than CMA-ES on the Ant-v1 task (Figure <a href="#S6.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Task setup. ‣ 6.2 Open-Ended Algorithm Discovery with The Agentic Scientist: Meta-Evolving CMA-Anchored Learned Evolution Strategies ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>).
Although the final GPT-5.6-sol + Codex and Kimi K3 + OpenCode candidates improve AUC over CMA-ES, their final Ant-v1 returns remain low:
Opus-5 + Claude and DeepSeek V4 Flash + Pi achieve the highest AUCs and terminal returns, whereas Kimi K3 yields the smallest AUC gain.
Claude’s highest-scoring candidate exceeds the dual-timescale diagonal innovation-memory strategy discovered by Codex in both AUC and terminal return. Next, we present the discoveries made by <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> using the previous Claude + Opus 5 setup. The detailed <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> paper is available in <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Learned Covariance Matrix Adaptation Paper &amp; AI Review ‣ Appendix C Highlighted Papers (Co-) Generated by The Agentic Scientist ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Strategy selected for the generated paper.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The system discovered <em id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">CMA-Anchored LearnedES</em>, which uses a separable-CMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ros and Hansen, 2008</a>)</cite> distribution <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=m+\sigma d\odot z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=m+\sigma d\odot z</annotation></semantics></math> and additionally augments the algorithm with three small shared MLPs containing 364 meta-evolved parameters:
A permutation-equivariant Deep Sets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zaheer et al., 2017</a>)</cite> module adjusts CMA recombination weights; global gates modulate mean and cumulative-step-size updates; and a coordinate-shared gate modulates diagonal covariance adaptation.
All learned outputs are bounded multiplicative residuals in <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\frac{1}{2},2]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\frac{1}{2},2]</annotation></semantics></math>; zero network outputs recover the separable-CMA update equations before the fixed sampling and re-expansion mechanisms described below.
The agent additionally implements fixed, horizon-free mechanisms around these learned gates (see <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Learned Covariance Matrix Adaptation Paper &amp; AI Review ‣ Appendix C Highlighted Papers (Co-) Generated by The Agentic Scientist ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>). These mechanisms are program structure rather than meta-evolved weights. Notably, the re-expansion cannot fire during the 50-generation BBOB inner loop, indicating an interplay between Ant-v1 validation and idea investigation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Post-search transfer across Brax tasks.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The manuscript drafted by <span id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> mentions the possibility of limited meta-transfer to some unseen tasks. Therefore, we test the selected Claude, Codex, and Pi programs on eight Brax-v1 environments using 16 new shared seeds: seven unseen environments and Ant as the search-validation reference environment.
The task setup differs from the meta-held-out setting: the test evaluation uses a zero-initialized affine–tanh policy, population 256, 2,000 generations, initial standard deviation 0.05, and 500-step episodes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F13" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/figures/metaevo_brax_comparison.png" id="S6.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:440/229;" width="440" height="229" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 13</span>: </span><span id="S6.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Post-search evaluation across eight Brax-v1 legacy-spring environments.
Curves show the mean best-so-far return over 16 shared seeds; shaded regions denote one standard error.
The grey Ant panel marks the search-validation reference environment, evaluated here with new seeds and the reduced transfer-policy interface; the other seven environments were unseen during agentic search.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While no method dominates on all environments (<a href="#S6.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Post-search transfer across Brax tasks. ‣ 6.2 Open-Ended Algorithm Discovery with The Agentic Scientist: Meta-Evolving CMA-Anchored Learned Evolution Strategies ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 13</span></a>; <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.2 Learned Covariance Matrix Adaptation Additional Results ‣ Appendix B The Agentic Scientist: Additional Results ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>)
the Opus-5 + Claude Code candidate matches or exceeds the mean terminal return of CMA-ES on 6 out of 8 environments and falls short on HalfCheetah and Hopper.
The DeepSeek V4 Flash + Pi candidate has the highest sample mean on HalfCheetah, but its margin over CMA-ES is smaller than the Pi candidate’s standard error.
The GPT-5.6-Sol + Codex candidate leads on Reacher and Walker2d.
We have released the discovered <em id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">CMA-Anchored LearnedES</em> optimizer for further study in <a href="https://github.com/RobertTLange/evosax/releases/tag/v.0.3.2" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">evosax v0.3.2</a> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lange, 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with <span id="S6.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span>:
<br class="ltx_break">Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we also evaluate <span id="S6.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> as a hill-climbing system for Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based language model fine-tuning.
Additionally, we provide several ablations on key configuration settings of <span id="S6.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> system.
In this setting, the system iteratively improves a training program through algorithmic modifications and hyperparameter tuning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task setup.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The task consists of optimizing the training procedure of a Qwen2.5-Math model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> on the MATH dataset from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al. (2021)</a></cite>.
We follow the task formulation of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Si et al. (2026)</a></cite>, in which each worker is initialized from a baseline Group Relative Policy Optimization  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>, GRPO,)</cite> training pipeline.
Our implementation is a re-engineered version of their reference code, restructured to integrate with the <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> sandbox, logging, and evaluation interfaces; the learning algorithm itself remains a faithful instantiation of GRPO.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F14" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:52%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/grpo_test_accuracies.svg" id="S6.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:253/157;" width="253" height="157"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="S6.F14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Post-search test accuracy of the best program of each GRPO run.
Each evaluation selects a run’s best program using the fixed validation set, evaluates it on the held-out test set across five seeds, and reports the mean and standard deviation.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Search and post-search evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> (Opus-4.7 + Claude) optimizes the accuracy on a validation set for 50 idea investigation iterations. During this search it never has access to the test set.
For each completed run, we keep the program with the highest validation accuracy, and rerun it on the full training and validation sets together, and then perform post-search evaluation on the test set (<a href="#S6.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Task setup. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 14</span></a>).
As shown in <a href="#S6.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Influence of the number of workers. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 15</span></a>, <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> iteratively improves validation accuracy from the GRPO baseline (<math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}\,52.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn> 52.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}\,52.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>) up to <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}\,71.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn> 71.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}\,71.9\%</annotation></semantics></math> in the best run.
In the post-search evaluation (<a href="#S6.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Task setup. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 14</span></a>), the best program of each run reaches up to <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="68.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>68.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy, well above the <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>47.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the initial program.
The aggressive hyperparameters selected by the best two-worker variant occasionally cause training to diverge during post-search evaluation, suggesting that they can overfit to validation outcomes and favor configurations whose gains do not transfer reliably to independent retraining.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Algorithmic changes in the best programs.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We find that the improvements discovered by <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> combine real algorithmic changes with hyperparameter tuning: <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> re-implements and combines several known techniques from the recent literature on RL fine-tuning.
These are not independent rediscoveries: <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> had in principle access to these techniques through web search, and they likely appeared in the underlying model’s training data.
The most common ones are the DAPO “clip-higher” rule <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, an asymmetric PPO clip with a larger upper bound, so that promising low-probability tokens are updated more strongly;
Dr. GRPO loss aggregation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which divides the loss by a fixed constant instead of the response length and thus removes the bias against long responses;
and GSPO-style importance ratios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, that is, a single length-normalized ratio per response instead of one per token.
Smaller changes include removing or simplifying the KL penalty, keeping only the prompt groups with mixed correct and incorrect answers, and penalizing overly long responses.
Overall, these changes show that hill-climbing over an RL fine-tuning program can not only tune hyperparameters but also select, re-implement, and combine relevant algorithmic ideas from the recent literature.
<span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> uses empirical feedback to decide which of these ideas to keep and how to combine them into training programs with higher accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Influence of the number of workers.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A recurring design choice across our experiments is the number of parallel workers spawned by the idea investigation stage of <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> at each iteration.
We study its effect on the RL fine-tuning task, running the system with 1, 2, and 4 parallel workers.
All worker configurations (<a href="#S6.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Influence of the number of workers. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 15</span></a>, Left) improve over the GRPO baseline validation accuracy (<math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}\,52.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn> 52.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}\,52.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>), with the 2-worker configuration reaching a validation accuracy of <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}\,66\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn> 66</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}\,66\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
Using multiple workers speeds up progress; for instance, the 2-worker variant reaches a score comparable to the 1-worker peak in less than half the wall-clock time, and effectively shares information between workers (<a href="#S6.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Influence of the number of workers. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 15</span></a>, Right).
Nonetheless, the benefit of parallelism is non-monotonic: using more workers does not necessarily yield better final results, suggesting that a small amount of parallel exploration injects useful diversity while larger pools can redundantly concentrate on similar local improvements.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F15" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/score_evo_grpo_several_workers.png" id="S6.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/137;" width="471" height="137" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F15.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 15</span>: </span><span id="S6.F15.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Search dynamics of <span id="S6.F15.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> on RL fine-tuning across three seeds per worker configuration.
<em id="S6.F15.7.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Left:</em> per-evaluation scores against iteration index and wall-clock duration.
<em id="S6.F15.7.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Right:</em> the combined 1- and 2-worker search tree per task, with examples of cross-worker inspirations relayed through shared memory. Small amounts of parallelism improve wall clock time and effectively transfer knowledge across workers. Further scaling of the parallelism does not show improvements.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-agent comparison.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A central question is how much performance comes from the orchestration introduced by <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> versus the underlying coding agent. While we partially address this question in <a href="#S5" title="5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we additionally compare Opus-4.7 + Claude Code, GPT-5.6-Sol + Codex, and Kimi K3 + Pi for the RL-based LLM fine-tuning task on the idea investigation phase in isolation.
Under this common setting, Pi achieves scores similar to Claude in a faster and more consistent manner, while reducing the API costs by 75%, and producing programs that generalize better to the post-search test dataset (<a href="#S6.F16" title="In Rubric-specification sensitivity. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>).
Codex, on the other hand, followed the task prompt instructions (<a href="#A7.SS5" title="G.5 Details of RL-based LLM fine-tuning ‣ Appendix G Task Properties and Hyperparameters ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.5</span></a>) more strictly: it never tuned hyperparameters after algorithmic changes, limiting the improvement process.
Overall, we conclude that the base model can have a significant impact on the idea investigation phase, including both final performance and search costs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rubric-specification sensitivity.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We observe a failure mode introduced by structural limitations of rubric-based verification: rubrics check only the criteria they enumerate, so they cannot catch violations of constraints that were never stated, and human researchers remain responsible for specifying tasks precisely and verifying that results respect their full intent.
In two of the three Pi runs, we observed that the agent also modified the test-time evaluation procedure itself (e.g., using <math id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-sample majority voting instead of the baseline’s pass@1), which inflates the reported validation accuracy without improving the training algorithm.
The task prompt asks the agent to improve the “training” algorithm, but never explicitly requires a fixed evaluation procedure. No initial rubric item covers this evaluation-protocol integrity. Neither the evaluator nor the rubric gates flagged these programs, and we identified them after a manual post-hoc audit.
After excluding protocol-violating programs, Pi still reaches high scores faster and more consistently than all other agents.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F16" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/score_evo_grpo_agents.svg" id="S6.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/137;" width="471" height="137"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F16.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 16</span>: </span><span id="S6.F16.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cross-agent comparison under the same orchestration scaffold across three seeds per agent.
<span id="S6.F16.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Left</span> to <span id="S6.F16.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Right</span>: score evolution during the search, test performance after reevaluation, and cumulative API cost per evolution cycle.
Crosses mark evaluations whose program modified the evaluation protocol (identified by manual audit); they are excluded from all running-best curves.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Influence of shared knowledge.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A second central design choice is the shared knowledge that connects all workers to a common memory of prior results, run summaries, and failure traces (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Parallel Investigation ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
To isolate its contribution, we compare our default 2-worker <span id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> to an ablated <em id="S6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no shared knowledge</em> variant, where each worker cannot see other workers’ conclusions and memory.
Shared knowledge improves the search process: the default configuration progresses faster, achieves a higher mean best-program score, and reduces the performance gap between workers (<a href="#S6.F17" title="In Influence of shared knowledge. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>, centre and right).
Nonetheless, we observe a substantial amount of inter-run variance.
The two variants reach similar final best scores across workers: the default configuration scores slightly higher, but the difference is not statistically significant (<a href="#S6.F17" title="In Influence of shared knowledge. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>, left).
Hence, independent workers can find strong programs without cooperation at the cost of slower overall runtime.
These results suggest that sharing successful ideas accelerates the search and allows lower-scoring workers to benefit from improvements found by others.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F17" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.18933v1/global_knowledge_ablation_grpo.svg" id="S6.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/134;" width="462" height="134"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F17.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 17</span>: </span><span id="S6.F17.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Effect of shared knowledge on 2-worker GRPO search across three seeds per configuration. Crosses mark evaluations from the no-shared-knowledge runs whose program modified the evaluation protocol (identified by manual audit); they are excluded from all running-best curves.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Evaluating <span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> on PaperBananaBench</h2>

<figure id="S7.F18" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.18933v1/figures/autoillustrate_side_by_side_example.png" id="S7.F18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/97;" width="429" height="97" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S7.F18.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 18</span>: </span><span id="S7.F18.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">autoillustrate<span id="S7.F18.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> applied to the Darwin Gödel Machine paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>: the editable diagram (left) and its corresponding enhanced figure (right).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a methodology description, <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> produces an editable <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> diagram and an enhanced figure derived from it (<a href="#S7.F18" title="In 7 Evaluating autoillustrate on PaperBananaBench ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>).
We evaluate the generated figures on PaperBananaBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, following the original evaluation protocol and using GPT-6-Astra as the VLM judge, as it more reliably penalizes small structural errors such as disconnected arrows (Figure <a href="#A5.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ E.2 Results with Gemini-3.1-Pro as VLM judge ‣ Appendix E autoillustrate: Supplementary Material ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>).
Results with Gemini-3.1-Pro as the judge are reported in <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Results with Gemini-3.1-Pro as VLM judge ‣ Appendix E autoillustrate: Supplementary Material ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.
Each generated diagram is compared to its human-designed equivalent with respect to four criteria: Faithfulness, Readability, Conciseness, and Aesthetics.
Each comparison receives 100 points when the generated diagram wins, 50 for a tie, and 0 when it loses.
The Overall score prioritizes fidelity and clarity over brevity and visual polish: a method wins overall if it wins at least one of Faithfulness and Readability without losing the other; if neither wins, Conciseness and Aesthetics are used to break the tie.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmark results.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Claude-based <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> pipeline achieves the highest Overall score, 37.5 against 25.0 for the best PaperBanana variant, driven by higher Faithfulness (<a href="#S7.T4" title="In Limitations: cost and runtime. ‣ 7 Evaluating autoillustrate on PaperBananaBench ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
All <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> variants generate on average more faithful figures, which is crucial for automated research since it forms the basis of method communication.
PaperBanana produces overly detailed diagrams, with higher chances of small image-generation errors.
Conciseness is more challenging for <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>, as the editable diagram primitives constrain compact and complex visual abstraction generation.
Although <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> remains below the human-reference Overall score of 50.0, its editable source files allow users to refine generated diagrams.
The Codex-based variant is on par with the Claude-based pipeline on Faithfulness and Conciseness, but scores lower on Readability and Aesthetics, as it tends to generate more cluttered diagrams.
Removing the panel inspections and final verification critics lowers Faithfulness and Overall scores, as these audits detect and repair factual inaccuracies with respect to the source methodology.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations: cost and runtime.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> variants generally have higher median API costs per diagram than PaperBanana, assuming raw API pricing.
Additionally, <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>’s median runtime is higher, as producing editable <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">draw.io</span> diagrams requires agents to write XML templates and Python programs that place elements, avoid collisions, and route arrows precisely, which demands substantial reasoning.
Within <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span>, removing the critics approximately halves runtime, and using low inference effort reduces runtime by a further 30%.</p>
</div>

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summary.</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across multiple research case studies, <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> demonstrates that coding agents can contribute to scientific research when embedded in an orchestrated workflow that preserves evidence and tests claims.
Our results span several levels of scientific autonomy, including a co-created Error Diffusion paper accepted at a conference, the fully autonomous discovery of structural inductive biases for Doc-to-LoRA, and a concrete CMA-anchored learned optimizer.
Complementing these detailed case studies, our cross-harness and model evaluation comprises 70 research campaigns across five manually prepared tasks and 14 harness-model configurations. The manuscript AI reviews show differences across model generations, and a positive trend toward newer models. With the same LLM base model, we observe no consistent differences across harnesses. Stronger task search performance predicts higher AI reviewer scores on 4 of 5 considered tasks.
This positions <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> as a human-steerable scaffold for end-to-end computational research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discussion.</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> and its experiments raise questions about the nature of scientific contributions on several levels: for the researcher, what to specify and how much autonomy to grant; for the generated artifacts, what a search score misses and how to validate generated research. We discuss each below:</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">From implementation to specification.</span>
As coding agents take over implementation, the human role shifts toward specifying the research contract: the task, its evaluators, and the rubrics that gate each stage.
This contract is also where failures can arise.
Agents may exploit what the contract leaves unstated: <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v1</span> edited its code to extend its own time limits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> changed the evaluation protocol on a subset of RL fine-tuning runs (<a href="#S6.F16" title="In Rubric-specification sensitivity. ‣ 6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>).
Furthermore, agents can follow the contract instructions too literally (<a href="#S6.SS3" title="6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.3</span></a>), requiring a subtle balance of scientific expression and concrete verifiability.
Since neither deviation is apparent from the reported numbers alone, precise specification and auditing become central research skills.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Autonomy spectrum.</span>
The <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v2</span> produced a fully AI-generated paper that passed peer review at a workshop before its pre-agreed withdrawal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The Error Diffusion paper, on the other hand, resulted from using <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> as a tool within a co-scientist setting.
The two modes are complementary: fully autonomous campaigns cheaply screen many directions, while human steering turns the most promising ones into verified contributions.
In the Error Diffusion project, this human effort was supplied throughout: defining the direction, baseline, and initial rubrics; verifying results, references, and claims; adding reinforcement-learning experiments; and clarifying notation and mechanisms after peer review (<a href="#S4" title="4 AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Beyond hill-climbing.</span>
A higher search score often does not by itself imply a better scientific contribution.
Although <a href="#S5.F9" title="In Search progress and rubric dynamics. ‣ 5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows that higher task scores tend to come with higher AI reviewer scores, the score hides two aspects of scientific contributions.
First, a single search objective can hide trade-offs: a richer sparse autoencoder encoder reduces reconstruction error but worsens a feature-perturbation metric, and a tabular deployment recipe raises balanced accuracy while lowering ordinary accuracy.
Second, a score gain can come from low-level engineering rather than high-level innovation: in RL fine-tuning of language models, gains came from re-implementing and combining existing techniques rather than from new mechanisms (<a href="#S6.SS3" title="6.3 RL-Based LLM Fine-Tuning with The Agentic Scientist:Studying the Effects of Agent Choice, Parallelism, and Shared Knowledge ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.3</span></a>).
Post-search ablations, analysis, and reporting expose the first; the second requires a provenance map that links ideas, hypotheses, and claims to prior work, extending the current claim-to-source map beyond experimental evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validating generated research.</span>
We evaluate research campaigns with several signals of different strength, each limited when viewed in isolation: AI reviewer scores, post-search transfer evaluations (such as unseen Brax environments in <a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Open-Ended Algorithm Discovery with The Agentic Scientist: Meta-Evolving CMA-Anchored Learned Evolution Strategies ‣ 6 Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>), and external peer review.
Peer review most directly assesses scientific merit but needs expert time for every manuscript, so it cannot cover all campaigns, while AI reviewer scores can potentially be overfit like any other metric.
Post-search transfer evaluations offer a scalable middle ground, provided they are fixed before search and held out from it.
Other signals could strengthen this evidence: Reviewers drawn from several model families to dilute the circularity of using the same models for investigation and rubric review <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; independent reproduction experiments behind each claim; and a measure of idea novelty, which previous signals do not capture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations.</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At present, <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> could be enhanced by a reliable literature-to-code pipeline for constructing state-of-the-art baselines.
The task drafting pipeline (<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Research Task Setup ‣ 3 The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>) is also not fully robust: it can draft simple tasks such as circle packing from a research brief, but for larger tasks such as the world-model and tabular distribution-shift tasks in <a href="#S5" title="5 Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, it may fail to produce an initial program, evaluators, and task contract that exactly match the full <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Agentic Scientist</span> scaffold.
Reliable task drafting nevertheless remains an important capability, since it removes the last manual step between a research brief and an automated campaign.
Unlike <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v1</span> and <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AI Scientist-v2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> only explicitly searches the literature during manuscript writing rather than during initial ideation. That being said, we repeatedly observe that coding agents leverage general web access to inform idea investigation.
Beyond these capability gaps, the system’s verification is only as complete as its task-specific evaluators and rubrics, which may omit methodological errors or reward unintended shortcuts.
Results that pass verification should therefore still be inspected and validated by human researchers.
Although the cross-harness and model evaluation covers 70 campaigns, its paper-level metric is an AI-reviewer proxy rather than full evidence of scientific correctness, and only the Error Diffusion paper underwent external peer review.
Our evaluations are also restricted to computational machine learning, so they do not establish the feasibility of transferring the orchestration workflow to domains requiring physical experiments or human-subject studies.
Finally, for <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">autoillustrate</span> we present additional component-specific limitations and failure cases in <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix E autoillustrate: Supplementary Material ‣ The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ethical considerations.</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">AI-assisted generation of research can create risks for attribution, research integrity, and an already constrained peer-review process.
We submitted only the single Error Diffusion paper for external review after human verification; the other generated manuscripts served as internal evaluation artifacts.
For the Error Diffusion paper specifically, human researchers verified its implementations, results, claims, and references, correcting unsupported claims and incomplete attribution before submission.
Responsible deployment also requires sandboxed execution, provenance for generated code and text, disclosure of agent contributions, watermarking of generated papers, and human accountability for safety, authorship, and final claims.
More broadly, researchers remain responsible for disclosing agent contributions and deciding whether generated work is suitable for submission and external review.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Future work.</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scientific progress often comes from exploring diverse “lottery tickets” across seemingly unrelated domains.
Applying <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> broadly could accelerate this process by screening a larger hypothesis space through greater compute within individual research directions and exploration of more directions within a topic.
To support human validation, the claim-to-source map should be exposed through an interface that lets researchers navigate from each claim to the experiments and results behind it.
The interface should also allow researchers to provide domain expertise and use the system as an interactive research tool.
Another improvement would be to automate the design of post-search transfer evaluations.
Where possible, rubric criteria should be implemented as automated tests, checked for reward hacking, and complemented by independent scientific review  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goel et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gunjal et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
With traceable evidence and enhanced rubrics, <span id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">The Agentic Scientist</span> could broaden and accelerate experimental search while leaving scientific judgment and responsibility with researchers.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
